title: SRE & Reliability
tagline: SLIs, SLOs, SLAs, error budgets, toil, incident response, and postmortems — the engineering discipline of keeping systems reliably available.

sections.content:
In 2003, Google had a problem that money alone could not solve. Their search infrastructure was growing faster than their ops team could manage it. The traditional approach — hire more system administrators and throw them at the pile of manual tasks — was not scaling. So Benjamin Treynor Sloss founded a new team with an unusual mandate: take software engineers and give them an operations responsibility, but enforce that at least 50% of their time must be spent on engineering work that makes operations better. He called the role **Site Reliability Engineer**, and the discipline that emerged from it — **SRE** — has since become one of the most influential frameworks in modern software operations.

The central insight of SRE is disarmingly simple: reliability is a **feature**, not a binary property. Instead of vaguely promising 'high availability', you measure exactly how reliable your system currently is, decide exactly how reliable it needs to be, and use the gap between those numbers to make engineering decisions. This reframes operations from a cost centre into a discipline with quantifiable goals and measurable progress.

The vocabulary that makes this concrete — **SLIs**, **SLOs**, **SLAs**, and **error budgets** — looks like corporate jargon at first glance. But these four concepts are tightly interlocked and form a decision-making engine: they tell you when to ship fast, when to slow down, what to monitor, and when an incident is truly serious. Combined with principled approaches to **toil reduction**, **incident response**, and **blameless postmortems**, they transform operations from reactive firefighting into a disciplined engineering practice.

This chapter builds that vocabulary from the ground up, shows how each concept connects to the others, and demonstrates how real SRE teams use error budgets as a negotiating tool between product velocity and operational reliability. Whether you are a backend engineer who gets paged occasionally or someone aspiring to an SRE role, these ideas will fundamentally change how you think about building systems that need to stay up.

sections.title: The Airline On-Time Budget
sections.content:
An airline promises passengers that 99% of flights will depart on time — that is their **SLA**, the contractual commitment with teeth. If they miss it, passengers get vouchers and regulators get unhappy. Internally, the operations team targets 99.5% — a tighter goal called the **SLO**. This buffer means they can breach their own internal target by 0.4 percentage points before the legal promise is in danger. The actual measurement they track — the percentage of departures within 15 minutes of schedule — is the **SLI**.

Now consider the 0.5% of allowed late flights. That is the airline's **error budget** for the month. It covers planned maintenance windows (gate closures for repairs), experiments with new boarding procedures, the occasional knock-on delay from weather, and any genuine failures. The budget is the allowance for imperfection and risk-taking.

Imagine it is day 20 of the month and they have only used 0.1% of that budget — they have 0.4% remaining. A product manager says: 'Let's trial a new luggage scanning system on Gate 7 this week. It might cause a few delays while staff learn it.' The ops team checks the budget and agrees: they have room to experiment. But if it is day 20 and they are already at 0.45%, the answer is: 'Not this month.' The budget has spoken.

**Toil** in this analogy is the gate agent who, every single morning, manually calls all 180 passengers to inform them of a delay rather than using the automated SMS system. The call content never changes; it does not get faster as passenger volume grows; it produces no improvement in the underlying process. It is purely manual, repetitive, and unscalable. The SRE principle says: build the SMS automation, and redirect that human energy to something that matters.

**Postmortems** are the debrief held the day after a major delay cascaded into five missed connections and three gate changes. The team assembles a timeline — what happened, when, what each system and person saw and did — and identifies the *systemic* conditions that made the cascade possible: an understaffed gate turnaround process, a missing escalation path, a broken inter-terminal communication channel. The debrief is explicitly not about blaming the gate agent who made the original call. That person acted reasonably given the information they had. The *system* created the conditions for failure, and the system is what needs to change.

sections.title: SLIs: What You Actually Measure
sections.content:
A **Service Level Indicator** is a quantitative measurement of some aspect of the service that is visible to users. The key word is *quantitative*: it is a number, not a feeling. SLIs must be precise enough that two engineers looking at the same data agree on the value.

The most common SLI categories are:

**Availability SLI** measures the fraction of requests that succeed. The precise definition matters enormously. 'Success' might mean HTTP 2xx response, or it might mean the response arrived within a timeout *and* contained valid data. Define it too loosely and you are measuring something users do not care about. A common formulation:

`availability = successful_requests / total_requests`

Measured over a rolling time window (usually 28 or 30 days) so that a single bad hour does not permanently destroy your monthly number, but also does not disappear instantly.

**Latency SLI** measures the fraction of requests that complete within a defined time threshold. This is almost always preferable to measuring *average* latency, because averages hide the long tail. A service where 95% of requests complete in 50ms and 5% take 10 seconds has a 'great' average but a terrible user experience. Define latency SLIs against a threshold: 'fraction of requests completing in under 200ms'.

**Quality SLI** is relevant for services where degraded responses are possible. A search engine that returns results but omits half the index is 'available' by availability SLI but delivering a degraded product. A quality SLI might measure 'fraction of responses that include results from all index shards'.

**Freshness SLI** applies to data serving: 'fraction of reads that return data less than 10 minutes old'. Critical for caches, data pipelines, and anything where stale data is harmful.

Good SLIs share several properties: they are **user-centric** (they measure something users actually experience), **aggregatable** (they can be computed over a time window), and **actionable** (when they degrade, engineers know what to investigate). Avoid SLIs that measure internal system properties like CPU usage — if the CPU is high but users are happy, the SLI should not fire.

sections.title: SLOs: The Internal Reliability Target
sections.content:
A **Service Level Objective** is a target value (or range) for an SLI, measured over a specific time window. It is an internal commitment — a promise the engineering team makes to itself. If the SLO is breached, engineering action is required, even if no SLA has been violated yet.

A well-formed SLO has three components: the SLI being targeted, the threshold, and the time window:

*'The availability SLI will be at or above 99.9%, measured over a rolling 28-day window.'*

The **time window** is important and often underspecified. Common choices:
- **Rolling window** (e.g. 'last 28 days'): the budget renews continuously, which gives smoother incentives and avoids the 'sprint to December 31 to use the remaining budget' problem.
- **Calendar window** (e.g. 'per calendar month'): simpler to explain to customers and business stakeholders, but creates perverse incentives at month end.

SLOs should be set based on **actual measured reliability**, not aspirational values plucked from air. The process: measure your current SLI over the past 90 days, find the level you were actually achieving, subtract a small buffer for noise, and set that as your starting SLO. Then tighten it incrementally as you improve reliability. Setting an SLO dramatically better than current reality means it will be breached constantly, destroying its credibility as a signal.

SLOs should also have **multiple latency targets**, not just one. The Google SRE Workbook recommends SLOs at multiple percentile thresholds: 'p50 < 100ms, p95 < 500ms, p99 < 2s'. Each percentile catches a different failure mode — the p50 catches systemic slowness affecting all traffic, while the p99 catches occasional catastrophic stalls affecting a small but vocal segment of users.

The **SLO tightness spectrum** creates a tension: a tighter SLO (99.99%) means less risk tolerance and fewer opportunities to experiment, but a looser SLO (95%) may mask real reliability problems. Choose the tightest SLO that your infrastructure can sustainably meet without heroic effort.

sections.title: SLAs: The Contractual Layer and Why It Must Be Looser
sections.content:
A **Service Level Agreement** is a legal or contractual commitment to customers (or between internal teams) that specifies the reliability the customer is paying for, and the consequences — usually financial credits or penalties — if that level is not met.

SLAs are almost always **looser** (lower percentage) than the corresponding internal SLO. This is not a cynical choice — it is a structural requirement. If your SLA equals your SLO, then any SLO breach is simultaneously a contractual breach with financial consequences. The SRE team would have no warning before legal penalties activate.

By setting SLA below SLO, you create a buffer zone:

`SLA = 99.5%` ← contractual floor; financial penalties if breached
`SLO = 99.9%` ← internal target; engineering action if breached

When the SLO is breached, engineers mobilise. The SLA is still intact. If engineering work restores reliability before the SLA is breached, customers never notice. The SLO breach was an early warning, not a crisis.

SLAs create a useful forcing function for *negotiation* between product, engineering, and business. Before signing an SLA with a customer, someone must ask: 'Can our SLO sustainably support this SLA?' If the answer is no, either the engineering work to raise the SLO must be prioritised, or the SLA terms must be relaxed. This makes reliability a business conversation, not just an engineering concern.

Some services have no external SLAs at all — internal tools, non-critical APIs. In those cases, SLOs still matter as internal calibration, but the 'SLA vs SLO' buffer is less critical.

sections.title: Error Budgets: Turning Reliability into a Decision Engine
sections.content:
The **error budget** is the fraction of time or requests that the service is *allowed* to be unreliable, as defined by the SLO:

`error_budget = 1 - SLO_target`

For a 99.9% availability SLO over a 30-day month (43,200 minutes):

`error_budget = 0.001 × 43,200 = 43.2 minutes`

That is the total downtime budget for the month. It gets consumed by everything that makes the service unavailable: incidents, planned maintenance windows, risky deployments that cause a brief degradation, and even legitimate production tests. The error budget is **shared** across all teams working on the service — product engineers shipping features and SRE engineers doing maintenance draw from the same pool.

This shared ownership is the mechanism that aligns incentives. Previously, product engineers wanted to ship as fast as possible (with little concern for reliability) while operations engineers wanted to ship as slowly as possible (to avoid incidents). Error budgets change the game: if there is plenty of budget left, both teams agree to ship fast. If the budget is nearly exhausted, both teams agree to slow down — because they share the consequences.

**Burn rate** is how fast you are consuming the budget relative to the expected pace. A burn rate of 1.0 means you are on track to exactly exhaust the budget by the end of the window. A burn rate of 14.4 on a 30-day SLO means you are consuming 14.4 months' worth of budget per month — at that rate, the full budget is gone in about 2 hours (30 days / 14.4 / 24 hours ≈ 2 hours). The **Google SRE Workbook** recommends using burn rate as the basis for alert severity:

- Burn rate > 14.4 over 1 hour → P1 alert (imminent budget exhaustion)
- Burn rate > 6 over 6 hours → P2 alert (significant erosion)
- Burn rate > 3 over 3 days → P3 alert (slow leak, needs investigation)

Multi-window burn rate alerts (checking both a short and long window simultaneously) reduce false positives while maintaining sensitivity to real problems.

**Budget-based deployment gates** are a direct application: if the error budget for the current window is more than 50% exhausted and there are still 15 days left, automated systems can block new deployments until the budget regenerates. This makes reliability enforcement automatic rather than dependent on human judgement under pressure.

The burn rate function reveals the key insight: an error rate of 1.44% on a 99.9% SLO (0.1% budget) means you are consuming the budget 14.4 times faster than expected — the P1 alert threshold because that pace exhausts the entire monthly budget in about 2 hours.

sections.title: Toil: The Enemy of Engineering Time
sections.content:
**Toil** is a specific SRE term for operational work with these properties: it is **manual** (a human must do it), **repetitive** (the same task recurs), **automatable** (a machine could do it instead), **tactical** (it does not move the system forward), and **scales linearly with service growth** (more traffic means proportionally more toil). Not all hard work is toil — designing a new alerting system is hard work but not toil, because it produces lasting improvement.

Examples of textbook toil:
- Manually restarting a service every morning because it gradually leaks memory.
- Running the same SQL query to unblock a stuck batch job twice a week.
- Manually provisioning a new database user every time a new developer joins.
- Responding to alert pages that are known false positives but have not been fixed.
- Hand-editing a config file and SSHing into servers to deploy it.

The operational harm of toil is not merely inefficiency. Toil has a **compounding cost**: as the service grows, toil grows with it. A manual step that takes 2 minutes per deploy is manageable at 10 deploys per week. At 100 deploys per week (a growing team, more microservices), the same step consumes 200 minutes per week — half an engineer-day. Meanwhile, every minute spent on toil is a minute not spent eliminating the next source of toil or building reliability improvements.

The Google SRE book enshrines **50% as the toil ceiling**: if more than half an SRE team's time is consumed by toil, it is a crisis requiring escalation and investment. The team should track toil explicitly — measuring it as a counter in the same way they measure request rates — so there is data to justify automation projects. 'We restart stalled workers 47 times per month; automating this saves 94 engineering-minutes monthly and eliminates a class of 2am pages.'

Toil elimination has a virtuous cycle: automating one task frees time to automate the next, which frees time for reliability engineering, which produces fewer incidents, which means fewer pages, which means fewer emergency toil spikes.

sections.title: Incident Response: Mitigate First, Diagnose Second
sections.content:
An incident is any event that significantly degrades the service's SLI. The severity hierarchy (P1/P2/P3/P4 or SEV1/SEV2 etc.) maps roughly to: how fast is the error budget burning? A P1 is burning budget fast enough to exhaust it within hours; a P4 is a noticeable but slow degradation.

The cardinal rule of incident response is **mitigation before diagnosis**. When a production system is failing, the instinct is to understand *why* before acting. Resist this. Users are impacted now. Every minute spent on root cause analysis while service is degraded is a minute of user pain. The first goal is to restore service, even if the 'restoration' is a rollback that throws away good work.

A well-functioning incident response process has these phases:

**Detect**: An automated alert fires, or a user report comes in. Monitoring should catch incidents before users report them — user reports indicate a monitoring gap.

**Triage**: Assess severity. Is this affecting all users or a subset? Is it a 100% error rate or 2%? Is the error budget burning at P1 rate? The triage determines the response posture.

**Declare**: For significant incidents (P1/P2), a formal incident is declared. An **Incident Commander (IC)** takes ownership of the coordination — they are not the person fixing the problem, they are the person keeping everyone organised, communicating with stakeholders, and preventing duplicate work.

**Communicate**: The status page is updated immediately with a vague-but-honest message: 'We are investigating elevated error rates affecting [service].' Communicating early — even before you understand the cause — reduces inbound support volume and manages expectations.

**Mitigate**: The technical responders work to restore service. Common mitigation strategies: roll back the most recent deploy, redirect traffic to a healthy region, increase the timeout on a backing service to reduce cascading failures, scale out to absorb load. The mitigation does not need to be the 'right' fix — it needs to stop the bleeding.

**Resolve**: Service is restored and stable. The formal incident is closed. Error budget consumption is recorded.

**Post-incident work**: Within 24-48 hours, a postmortem is written. Action items are created.

**Runbooks** are pre-written step-by-step guides for common incidents. A runbook for 'database connection pool exhausted' tells the on-call engineer exactly which dashboard to check, which query to run, how to identify which service is holding connections, and what the escalation path is. Good runbooks transform a panicked midnight response into a methodical process.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The `checkBurnRateAlert` function embodies the Google SRE Workbook's multi-threshold approach. Dividing the current error rate by the SLO's allowed error rate gives burn rate directly. The P1 threshold of 14.4x is chosen because 1/14.4 = 0.069 — at that rate, a 30-day budget depletes in about 2 hours, requiring immediate human response. The toil counter makes the 'automate worker restarts' argument data-driven: when the Grafana dashboard shows 47 restarts per month, the ticket to add a Kubernetes liveness probe writes itself.

sections.title: Blameless Postmortems: Learning Without Punishment
sections.content:
A **blameless postmortem** is a structured written analysis completed after every significant incident. The 'blameless' aspect is not about excusing bad behaviour — it is about recognising that complex systems fail due to combinations of conditions, not the simple mistake of one person. When a system is designed such that a single human error can trigger a P1 outage, the design is the problem.

The philosophical foundation comes from human factors research (particularly Sidney Dekker's work on 'New View' safety thinking): people act rationally given the information, tools, and constraints they have at the time. If a deploy caused an outage, asking 'why did the engineer push that?' is less useful than asking 'why was the deployment process designed such that this particular change could reach production without catching the problem?'

A well-structured postmortem contains:

**Title and metadata**: Date, incident ID, severity, duration, author, reviewers.

**Impact**: Concrete numbers. 'Approximately 12,000 users could not complete checkout for 19 minutes. Estimated revenue impact: $47,000.'

**Timeline**: A precise chronological reconstruction of events, including both what happened in the system and what engineers observed and did. Timestamps matter. Gaps in the timeline are findings.

**Root cause analysis**: Usually multiple contributing factors, not one root cause. The '**5 Whys**' technique is common: ask 'why' repeatedly until you reach a systemic, addressable cause. 'The deploy caused a spike in DB connections (Why?) because the new query ran without index (Why?) because the code review did not include query plan review (Why?) because our review checklist does not require it (Why?) because we have never had an index-related incident before.' The last answer points to the fix: add query plan review to the checklist.

**Contributing factors**: Conditions that made the incident worse or harder to diagnose. Missing runbook. Alert fired 3 minutes late. No canary deployment process.

**Action items**: Concrete, owner-assigned, deadline-bound tasks. 'Add index on `orders.user_id` — @backend-alice — by April 1.' Not vague ('improve deployment process') — specific and measurable.

The cultural effect of blameless postmortems over time is significant: engineers stop hiding incidents, start reporting near-misses (incidents that almost happened), and feel safe escalating problems early because doing so produces learning rather than punishment.

sections.title: Monitoring, Alerting, and the Four Golden Signals
sections.content:
Effective SRE practice requires a monitoring foundation that gives SLI data in real time and fires alerts calibrated to error budget consumption. The Google SRE book defines **four golden signals** as the minimum useful monitoring set for any service:

**Latency**: The time it takes to serve a request. Track the *distribution* (p50, p95, p99, p999), not the mean. Latency degradation often precedes availability degradation — it is an early warning sign.

**Traffic**: The demand being placed on your system — requests per second, messages per second, transactions per second. Traffic context makes other signals interpretable: a 1% error rate at 10 RPS (1 error per 100 seconds) is very different from 1% at 10,000 RPS (100 errors per second).

**Errors**: The rate of requests that fail — explicitly (5xx responses), implicitly (2xx responses with wrong data), or by policy (responses too slow to be useful). This feeds the availability SLI directly.

**Saturation**: How full is the service? CPU at 90%, memory at 85%, disk at 95%, connection pool at 95% capacity. Saturation predicts future failures before they manifest as errors. A service at 95% CPU can absorb a 5% traffic spike; a service at 99% CPU cannot.

**Alert design** should be SLO-driven, not threshold-driven. Instead of alerting on 'CPU > 80%' (which may be irrelevant), alert on 'error budget burn rate > 14.4x over the past 1 hour'. This directly answers: 'Is the user experience degrading faster than our SLO allows?' CPU at 95% with 0% errors is not a user-visible problem. A 2% error rate with CPU at 50% is.

The practical consequence: **fewer, more actionable alerts** that are deeply tied to user experience, rather than many threshold-based alerts that create alert fatigue and cause real incidents to be missed in the noise.

sections.title: SRE Organisational Patterns and Common Pitfalls
sections.content:
SRE exists in several organisational forms depending on company size and maturity:

**Embedded SRE**: One or two SREs join a product team. They own the reliability posture of that service, define SLOs, build monitoring, and work directly with product engineers on reliability. This is common in mid-sized companies where a dedicated SRE team is not yet justified.

**Central SRE team**: A separate SRE organisation that provides reliability infrastructure (monitoring platforms, deployment tooling, runbook templates) to all product teams, and onboards critical services. Product teams must meet an 'SRE acceptance bar' — defined SLOs, comprehensive runbooks, evidence of chaos engineering — to receive SRE support.

**'You build it, you run it'**: Each product team is fully responsible for their own reliability with SRE providing only tooling and consultation. This is the DevOps model. SRE principles (SLOs, error budgets, postmortems) apply fully, but there is no separate SRE headcount.

Common pitfalls when implementing SRE:

**Setting SLOs in meetings without data**: SLOs derived from aspiration rather than measurement are immediately breached and lose credibility. Always start with 90-day historical SLI data.

**100% SLO targets**: Impossible, paralysing, and counterproductive. Any deployment creates some risk of a brief degradation. A 100% SLO means no deployments are safe. Embrace the error budget.

**Ignoring toil until it explodes**: Toil grows silently. Teams that do not measure it are often shocked to discover they are spending 70-80% of time on it. Measure toil monthly.

**Blame-ful postmortems**: If engineers fear punishment, they hide incidents, avoid escalating, and write sanitised postmortems that protect individuals but miss the systemic issues. Psychological safety is not optional — it is mechanically required for postmortems to produce useful findings.

**Alert fatigue**: Too many alerts that are not tied to user impact. Engineers start silencing pages or auto-acking alerts. When the real P1 fires, it gets lost in the noise.

**Historical context**: The term 'Site Reliability Engineering' was coined by Ben Treynor Sloss at Google in 2003. Google published 'Site Reliability Engineering' (2016) and 'The Site Reliability Workbook' (2018) — both free online — which codified the practices and spread them industry-wide. The concepts of error budgets and blameless postmortems were heavily influenced by earlier work in the aviation and nuclear industries on high-reliability organisations (HROs), where safety and operational continuity had been formalised for decades before software adopted the language.

**Interview and exam traps**: When asked about SLOs, always distinguish them from SLAs — interviewers specifically probe this. Know the error budget formula cold: `(1 - SLO) × window_minutes`. When asked 'what do you do when an incident occurs?', lead with mitigation before root cause — this is the answer that signals SRE experience. For the burn rate question: 14.4x on a 30-day window = full budget in 2 hours — know this number. Finally, when discussing postmortems, emphasise that 'blameless' does not mean 'consequence-free for genuine negligence' — it means the *analysis* focuses on systemic conditions, not individual fault.

items: **SLI** is a specific quantitative metric representing user experience (e.g. fraction of successful requests). **SLO** is your internal reliability target for that SLI (e.g. 99.9% over 30 days). **SLA** is the contractual promise to customers — always set *looser* than the SLO to create a safety buffer before financial penalties activate.

**Error budget** = `(1 - SLO_target) × window`. For 99.9% over 30 days: 43.2 minutes per month. It is shared across all teams and consumed by incidents, maintenance, and risky deploys — it is the mechanism that aligns product velocity with reliability.

**Burn rate** measures how fast the error budget is depleting. A burn rate above 14.4x on a 30-day window means the full budget will be gone in approximately 2 hours — the threshold for a P1 alert requiring immediate response.

**Toil** is manual, repetitive, automatable operational work that scales with service growth. The SRE principle caps toil at 50% of engineering time; the rest must go to eliminating toil and improving reliability systems.

**Incident response** always prioritises mitigation (restore service) over diagnosis (find root cause). Roll back first, investigate second. An Incident Commander coordinates communication and prevents duplicate work while technical responders act.

**Blameless postmortems** analyse system and process failures — not individual human error — and produce concrete, owner-assigned action items. Psychological safety is mechanically required: without it, engineers hide incidents and postmortems produce nothing useful.

The **four golden signals** — latency, traffic, errors, saturation — form the minimum useful monitoring foundation. Alert on error budget burn rate rather than raw thresholds to reduce alert fatigue and ensure every page corresponds to real user impact.

quiz.question: A service has a 99.9% availability SLO over a 30-day month. How many minutes of allowed downtime does the error budget represent?
options: 4.32 minutes
43.2 minutes
432 minutes
0 minutes — 99.9% means effectively zero downtime
quiz.explanation: Error budget = (1 - 0.999) × 30 × 24 × 60 = 0.001 × 43,200 = 43.2 minutes. This is the total allowable downtime before the SLO is breached for the month. Option A is off by 10x; option C is off by 10x in the other direction.

quiz.question: Why must an SLA target always be set lower (looser) than the internal SLO?
options: SLAs use different measurement units than SLOs, so a conversion factor is needed.
An SLO breach triggers early engineering action before the SLA is violated, preventing financial penalties from ever activating.
Customers cannot understand percentages above 99%, so SLAs are capped at 99%.
The SLO is set by the SRE team; the SLA is set by sales and is always more ambitious.
quiz.explanation: SLO (e.g. 99.9%) is tighter than SLA (e.g. 99.5%). When the SLO is breached, engineers mobilise immediately. This buffer means the team almost never breaches the SLA — so the financial penalties attached to SLA violations rarely (or never) trigger. Without this gap, any SLO breach would simultaneously be a contractual breach.

quiz.question: Which of the following is the best definition of an SLI?
options: The legal contract between the service provider and its customers, specifying financial penalties.
A specific, quantitative metric that represents some aspect of user-visible service quality, such as the fraction of successful requests.
The internal team target for reliability over a specific time window.
An automated tool that generates SLOs from application logs.
quiz.explanation: An SLI is the raw measurement — 'What fraction of requests returned a 2xx status in the last 28 days?' The SLO is the target for that metric. SLIs must be carefully chosen to reflect what users actually experience, not internal system properties like CPU utilisation.

quiz.question: A team's error budget is 85% consumed with 12 days remaining in the 30-day window. According to SRE principles, what is the correct response?
options: Ship the remaining planned features immediately to maintain business velocity before the budget resets.
Disable monitoring for the rest of the month to avoid consuming more budget on false-positive alerts.
Halt risky deployments and redirect engineering effort toward reliability improvements to avoid exhausting the remaining 15%.
Retroactively reclassify some downtime as 'planned maintenance' to restore the budget artificially.
quiz.explanation: With 85% of the budget consumed and 40% of the window remaining, you are on pace to exhaust the full budget well before month end. The SRE response is to freeze risky changes (new feature deployments) and focus on reliability. Options A, B, and D all destroy the signal that the error budget provides.

quiz.question: Which of the following is the clearest example of 'toil' in SRE?
options: Writing a runbook for a newly discovered failure mode.
Manually restarting a microservice every morning because it reliably leaks memory overnight.
Designing a new auto-scaling policy for the production cluster.
Conducting a blameless postmortem after a P1 incident.
quiz.explanation: Toil is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, and scales with service growth. Daily manual restarts are classic toil: the same action repeats indefinitely with no lasting improvement. The fix is either patching the memory leak or adding a liveness probe for automatic restart — both of which eliminate the toil permanently.

quiz.question: During an active production incident, what is the first engineering priority according to SRE principles?
options: Identify the root cause before taking any action to ensure the fix is permanent.
Notify all engineering managers and the CEO via email before making any system changes.
Mitigate the impact and restore service as quickly as possible — even by rolling back — before conducting any root cause analysis.
Update the SLO dashboard to reflect the current error budget consumption rate.
quiz.explanation: Mitigation (restore service) always comes before diagnosis (root cause analysis). Rolling back a recent deploy often restores service in minutes while the investigation continues afterward. Every minute spent on root cause analysis while users are impacted is additional budget consumption and user pain.

quiz.question: What does it mean for a postmortem to be 'blameless'?
options: No one is permitted to discuss who was involved in the incident — all names are redacted.
The analysis focuses on systemic conditions, process gaps, and tooling failures rather than attributing fault to individual engineers.
The postmortem document is kept confidential so team members do not feel embarrassed.
Action items from the postmortem are assigned to automated bots rather than individual humans.
quiz.explanation: Blameless postmortems assume that engineers acted rationally given their information, tools, and processes. The analysis targets the systemic conditions that made the incident possible — so future engineers don't face the same trap. Psychological safety is mechanically required: if engineers fear blame, they hide incidents and postmortems produce sanitised, useless findings.

quiz.question: A burn rate of 14.4x on a 99.9% SLO with a 30-day window means:
options: The service has already exceeded its error budget for the month.
At the current error rate, the full 30-day error budget will be exhausted in approximately 2 hours.
14.4% of all requests are currently failing.
The service has been continuously unavailable for 14.4 minutes.
quiz.explanation: Burn rate = current_error_rate / budget_error_rate. At 14.4x burn, you consume a full monthly budget in 30 days / 14.4 ≈ 2.08 days — but the standard multi-window approach checks the 1-hour window: 1 month / 14.4 / (24 × 30 hours) ≈ 2 hours. This is why 14.4x is the canonical P1 threshold in the Google SRE Workbook.

quiz.question: Why is a 100% availability target the wrong SLO to set?
options: Monitoring tools are incapable of measuring availability above 99.99%.
A 100% SLO means zero allowable downtime, making every deployment a potential SLO breach, paralyzing engineering velocity, and creating a promise that is physically impossible to keep.
Customers cannot distinguish between 99.9% and 100% availability, so the target is meaningless.
Setting 100% availability requires exactly twice as many on-call engineers.
quiz.explanation: A 100% SLO creates a zero-error-budget situation. Any deployment, maintenance window, or minor degradation immediately breaches it. This paralyses innovation, makes every change a crisis, and is impossible to sustain — even the most reliable infrastructure has planned maintenance. Error budgets exist because some unreliability is acceptable and should be spent wisely.

quiz.question: Which of the four golden signals would most directly feed into an availability SLI calculation?
options: Saturation — because a saturated system eventually becomes unavailable.
Latency — because slow responses indicate the system is struggling.
Errors — because the fraction of failing requests is directly the inverse of availability.
Traffic — because higher traffic increases the probability of failure.
quiz.explanation: Availability SLI = (total_requests - failed_requests) / total_requests, so the errors signal feeds it directly. Saturation and latency are leading indicators of future availability problems, and traffic provides context, but the errors signal is the direct input to the availability SLI calculation.
